column1: # .github/auth-register.tsv — one canonical authentication method per cell,
# and every second method that is allowed to exist alongside it.
# Rows are written BY HAND. Recompute fingerprints and line numbers with:
# The rule, the four conditions a justification must meet, the anchor forms
# and what the gate fails on: scripts/auth-register.sh
# revisit: a CHECKABLE FACT. A date is never a trigger, and the gate says so.
# anchor: go:<path>#<Symbol> | text:<path>#<literal> | none: (needs a cite)
# 'line' is navigation only and is refreshed each run; it is NOT part of the
# fingerprint, so edits above a row do not churn this file. Editing the
# ANCHORED declaration does change the fingerprint, and the gate then fails
# until someone re-reads the row against the code that changed.
# This file is PUBLIC. A row describing a fail-open that is unfixed and
# reachable does not belong here; it lives in a private geekdojo-brain issue
# and moves here in the pull request that fixes it.

column4: cell
column5: method
column6: exception
column7: constraint
column9: revisit

column4: browser to api, authenticate, HTTPS
column5: A discoverable passkey issues an opaque session. The session token is stored as its sha256 hash, and user verification is required.

column4: origin enforcement, HTTPS and WSS
column5: One normalized origin allowlist feeds WebAuthn, CORS, the WebSocket origin check and cross-origin protection. The security header set ships with it and carries no HSTS.

column4: first-run surface, HTTPS
column5: One fail-closed predicate (no claim row and no pre-update `users` row; a read error is "not first run") used by status, the launcher, restore candidates, restore phase 1 and the setup probe; the claim is one insert carrying both clauses and naming the earliest-created account.

column4: node to control plane, client auth, NATS
column5: A join token bound to the node id and to the role at mint, re-read on every connect. A token carrying no role never validates.

column4: node to control plane, server auth, NATS
column5: The bus key's SPKI pin, on a bus that accepts only TLS. One resolver reads it, in order, from the seeded environment value, from the pin file an earlier agent saved when the controlplane delivered it, and — on the controlplane's own agent alone — from the pin file its api writes at every start; the controlplane's file is read again on every handshake, so a restored bus key reaches its running agent, and every other source is fixed for the life of the process (geekdojo/geekdojo-brain#669). A node with no usable pin from any source does not dial the bus at all: there is no plaintext bus to fall back to (geekdojo/geekdojo-brain#517).

column4: revocation, every protocol
column5: One fact revokes: the token row is revoked, or the node is removed. Today that revokes the token and closes every live bus session it authenticated, and the node stays in inventory so its records remain analysable. Widening the cascade to HTTPS, the tailnet and the leaf files is tracked, not done. Ending a person's access is one Job, `identity.revoke`: online identity sessions, then offline sessions, then the change, then the api's console rows and a moved person's old rows, then the private-network device, app and network hooks, each step a recorded outcome.

column4: sidecar to api callbacks, HTTP
column5: None. The api reads alert state from VictoriaMetrics in a background loop; there is no inbound callback to authenticate.

column4: secrets at rest, filesystem
column5: Every secret file is written 0600 through a synced temporary file and a rename, with the mode set by fchmod rather than inherited from a umask. Modes are per file and no unit sets a UMask. One helper per Go module owns that decision (E36).

column4: detached CMS signatures, artifact
column5: artifactsig verification for an explicit purpose, with the purpose OID fixed per artifact class.

column4: operator to node shell, SSH
column5: One Go validator for the operator public key, shared by every surface that accepts one.

column4: human trust in the controlplane CA, out of band
column5: Trust on first use, for every device. There is no fingerprint comparison surface.

column4: anti-rollback, artifact
column5: One version-admission gate for the OS, the firewall and the catalog. No downgrade override.

column4: update bundle trust, artifact
column5: One verifier resolved from the trust root, with no permissive mode to select. Construction never returns an error, so there is no error path a caller can mishandle back into permissiveness: an absent, unreadable or unparseable root yields an unavailable verifier that refuses every artifact and carries the reason.

column4: external device server auth, HTTPS
column5: One pinned-TLS helper, with one typed pin: the SHA-256 of the DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo, in the same encoding as the bus pin. Verification runs in VerifyConnection, so it also runs on a resumed connection. There is no unpinned mode and no http endpoint.

column4: human at a node console, authenticate, local TTY and BMC serial
column5: One password, chosen by the operator in the first-run wizard and held only as a crypt(3) SHA-512 hash. No image bakes one. A job applies the hash to every node in inventory over that node's own command lane, and a node that enrols later is converged the same way. A node that cannot apply it fails with a reason and is never skipped.

column4: node to control plane, server auth, HTTPS
column5: The agent's HTTPS clients (bundle download, backup transfer, restore fetch) verify the api by chain to the node's trust bundle (the controlplane CA, plus the operator's CA on an external Headscale) and nothing else: no system roots, no pin. The bundle is re-read on every call, and a missing or unusable bundle refuses.

column4: collector to api, server auth, HTTPS
column5: The collector verifies the api's leaf by chain to the controlplane CA, under the cluster name. No certificate is pinned.

column4: node to control plane, client auth, HTTPS
column5: A key the node registered, admitted by its SPKI at the api's node listener, with the key's purpose checked per route. A backup transfer grant (rbx1) is per-object scope only: the node it names must be the key's owner.

column4: api to secret store, server auth, HTTPS
column5: The api verifies the store by chain to the store CA alone, over TLS 1.3 to a loopback IP literal with an explicit port. No system roots and no pin; a CA PEM holding no certificate refuses, and the client follows no redirect and reads no proxy or BAO_* setting.

column4: api to secret store, client auth, TLS
column5: The api presents a store-CA clientAuth leaf, CN rasputin-api, read from disk at each handshake and renewed by the one leaf sweep. A leaf that is absent or unreadable refuses the call with no request sent; a refused certificate is ErrDenied.

column4: seal rotation to secret store, client auth, TLS
column5: The seal-key rotation job logs in through the store's cert auth as its own role, rasputin-seal-rotate, presenting a store-CA clientAuth leaf with that CommonName that is minted for each handshake and never written to disk. The role's only policy is update and sudo on sys/rotate/root. A mint that fails refuses the call with no request sent; a refused certificate or login is ErrDenied.

column4: store provisioner to secret store, client auth, TLS
column5: The store provisioner (rasputin-os's rasputin-store-provision oneshot) presents a store-CA clientAuth leaf, CN rasputin-provisioner, minted and renewed by the api's one leaf sweep and delivered to the oneshot by LoadCredential=, so only the store's unit user and root read the copy. The store's rasputin-provisioner cert role admits only that CommonName and binds only the rasputin-provisioner policy, with token_no_default_policy set.

column4: store provisioner to secret store, server auth, HTTPS
column5: The store provisioner's bao client verifies the store by chain to the store CA alone, the store-ca.pem credential its unit loads (BAO_CACERT), over TLS to 127.0.0.1:8200, with every call bounded by BAO_CLIENT_TIMEOUT and no retry. The client is rasputin-os's usr/lib/rasputin/store-provision/rasputin-store-provision.sh, so nothing in this repo anchors it.

column4: api to secret store, authenticate, HTTPS
column5: The api logs in through the store's cert auth method as the rasputin-api role, presenting its store-CA client leaf, and holds the token in memory only. It logs in only when it holds no token, or when the store refuses (403 or a refused client certificate) a token an earlier call obtained; it then logs in once more and retries that call once, so each call makes at most one login. Every other failure keeps the token. It reads no TTL and starts no timer: the role's token_ttl (1h, set by the image's self-init) is a safety net over the facts every login re-checks, the client leaf and the role's CommonName pin.

column4: Super4C BMC, client and server auth, HTTPS
column5: The board admits a client only on a chain to the controlplane CA seeded into it, plus CN exactly rasputin-bmc-client, plus the clientAuth EKU, over TLS 1.3, and fails closed on anything else. It presents a controlplane-CA serverAuth leaf over a key it generated itself, which the client verifies by chain under the name the control plane gives the leaf when it signs it, bmc-<12 hex of its MAC>.<cluster id>.internal. Chain validation is dateless, because the board has no trusted clock. The check is geekdojo/rasputin-super4c-bmc components/bmc_core/authz.c#authz_allow, so nothing in this repo anchors it.

column4: api to identity service, server auth, HTTPS
column5: The api verifies the identity service by chain to the identity CA alone, over TLS 1.3 to 127.0.0.1:8543, whose serverAuth leaf carries IP SAN 127.0.0.1 and nothing else. No system roots, no pin and no controlplane CA. The api mints and renews the leaf in its one leaf sweep; a renewal restarts keycloak.service.

column4: api to identity service, client auth, TLS
column5: The api presents an identity-CA clientAuth leaf, CN rasputin-api, which the identity service's administrator client authenticates by client-x509 on its exact subject. Relayed browser traffic carries the door's identity-CA leaf, CN rasputin-door, which no administrator client accepts. Both leaves renew in the one leaf sweep.

column4: api to identity service, Admin API session, HTTPS
column5: The api logs in to realm rasputin as rasputin-admin by client-x509 (C27), with a client_credentials request that carries no secret, and holds the access token in memory only. It logs in only when it holds no token, or when the Admin API answers 401 to a token an earlier call obtained; it then logs in once more and retries that call once, so each call makes at most one login. Every other failure keeps the token. It never reads the token's exp and starts no timer: the token's lifespan is a safety net over the facts every login re-checks, the client leaf and the client's exact subject. The retry rule is the store session's (C24), one copy in tokensession.

column4: app to its own secrets at runtime, unix socket TLS
column5: A granted app's identity is a per-app relay socket the node's agent bind-mounts into that app's containers only; a call that arrives on it is that app, and the agent stamps the app's id on it. The app verifies the agent by chain to the controlplane CA alone, mounted beside the socket, under relay.rasputin.internal, over TLS 1.3; the agent's key is generated on the node and the api signs it at every deploy. The api refuses an app that does not exist, is not on the publishing node or is not granted, and the app may create, read, replace and delete only entries under apps/<id>/_runtime/. Removed at delete and with the node.

column4: identity service to its database, server auth, TLS
column5: Keycloak verifies PostgreSQL by chain to the identity CA alone, with pgjdbc's sslmode=verify-full against 127.0.0.1, the identity-db-server serverAuth leaf's only IP SAN, over TLS 1.3 (the server's ssl_min_protocol_version). Both sides read their files from their own unit's LoadCredential= copies. The api mints and renews the leaf in its one leaf sweep; a renewal restarts keycloak-db.service.

column4: identity service to its database, client auth, TLS
column5: Keycloak presents the identity-CA clientAuth leaf CN keycloak, its key written as unencrypted DER PKCS-8 for pgjdbc, and PostgreSQL's only pg_hba.conf line, hostssl keycloak keycloak 127.0.0.1/32 cert, maps that CommonName to the keycloak role. No password exists, and no Unix socket is opened.

column4: relying party to identity service, server auth, HTTPS
column5: The relying party verifies the identity service by chain to the controlplane CA under the door's own name: signin.<cid>.internal at the app door, sso-<cid>.local at the home door. Each name is on its own one-name leaf with no IP address, minted from the door table and renewed by the one leaf sweep, and no certificate is pinned. Both doors are served on :443, each chosen by SNI with its own leaf and a request whose SNI and Host name different sites refused with 421 (api.NewSites, geekdojo/geekdojo-brain#986); apps are handed the CA by Identity 7.3.

column4: browser to identity service, authenticate, HTTPS
column5: Username and password through one realm flow of stock authenticators, its variants bound per client.

column4: browser to api, authenticate, HTTPS
column5: The console is an OIDC client, rasputin-console, of the home door: an authorization-code flow with PKCE S256, a state, a nonce, prompt=login and the RFC 9207 iss check. The code is exchanged on loopback over the api leaf, the ID token is verified with go-oidc (T160), and an opaque console session is minted whose cookie is stored only as its sha256 hash. No token the identity service issued is kept. Supersedes C01.

column4: origin enforcement, HTTPS and WSS
column5: One normalized origin allowlist feeds CORS, the WebSocket origin check, cross-origin protection and the pre-update passkey ceremony. It never holds a sign-in door's origin. Supersedes C02.

column4: identity service to api, back-channel logout, HTTPS
column5: A logout token from the client's issuer, verified with go-oidc's VerifyLogout (signature, issuer, audience, expiry, the back-channel event, no nonce) and required to carry a sid, posted over the api leaf's TLS. It ends every console session of that sid (N5, Identity 7.5).

column4: administrator to account, password reset, HTTPS
column5: An administrator sets a temporary password as a Job at a fresh sign-in; the password travels beside the Job, never in its spec; every session of the target ends; before they end, a privileged target's privileged levels are recorded as its designation and taken away, and accounts.grant_designated_role returns them once its setup is complete.

column4: browser to identity service, create account, HTTPS
column5: Self sign-up at the home door (prompt=create for rasputin-console only), from home-network addresses that are neither tailnet nor node addresses, while fewer than 20 accounts wait for access, the cap held across account creation; a removed and an in-use email get one answer. The first account created is designated the first administrator (C03); every later one starts with no role and no access.

column4: root on the control plane to api, repair code, unix socket TLS
column5: The peer's uid, read from the kernel (SO_PEERCRED), is the authentication: only uid 0 is served, and any other connection is closed before TLS. TLS 1.3 with the api's identity-repair-code leaf, which the command verifies by chain to the identity CA under repair-code.rasputin.invalid; the socket sits in a 0700 root directory, and only the code's SHA-256 crosses it.

column4: browser to identity service, authenticate, HTTPS
column5: Username and password through one realm flow of stock authenticators, its variants bound per client (C40).
column6: A discoverable passkey alone, with user verification, signs in at the door it was made for.
column7: A passkey is scoped to its door's RP ID and user verification is required, so it is no weaker than the password and second step it replaces; it is the one-tap option inside the password form, not a second flow.
column9: D8's set of add-ons changes.

column4: browser to identity service, second step, HTTPS
column5: Username and password through one realm flow of stock authenticators, its variants bound per client (C40).
column6: After the password: a passkey or security key made at this door, or an authenticator code once the clock-sync fact holds; a recovery code stands in only for an account that holds one of those (C29).
column7: It is asked only where usable, by the per-door markers, and for a privileged account at either door; a privileged account with no second step at a door is denied with a sentence, never offered setup (C3, C22).
column9: D8's set of add-ons changes.

column4: browser to identity service, token issuance, HTTPS
column5: Username and password through one realm flow of stock authenticators, its variants bound per client (C40).
column6: The app access gate is a flow step, not a token policy.
column7: It is an attribute condition that fails closed: an account whose attribute is missing or does not match is denied with its sentence, on a password and on a cookie sign-in alike.
column9: Keycloak gains a per-client token policy, or D16 adopts a token-time check.

column4: browser to identity service, session, cookie
column5: A state change follows a checkable fact, never a clock.
column6: Identity-service sessions end after 30 idle minutes or 10 hours, remember-me off, and a credential change asks for the password again after 5 minutes (N8).
column7: An abandoned browser emits no fact; the bounds were ratified by Bryce on 2026-11-02 (D22). They decide only how soon someone retypes credentials; the console never reuses the session.
column9: A signed-in device emits a fact when abandoned.

column4: browser to api, session, cookie
column5: A console session ended by facts: sign-out, a back-channel logout of its identity session, a change to the account's roles, and the account seams of Identity 4.9 and 4.12. A break-glass repair session ended by facts: the operator ending it, an administrator's normal sign-in, a newer redemption, and an api restart (geekdojo/geekdojo-brain#321).
column6: A 7-day absolute lifetime also ends it.
column7: A lost or retired device produces no fact the api can observe, so no checkable fact is available to end that session. Repair sessions take the same bound (geekdojo/geekdojo-brain#321, auth.SessionLifetime, timer-audit L80), and Your account sessions do when geekdojo/geekdojo-brain#319 lands (D22). Supersedes E3.
column9: A signed-in device emits a fact the api can observe when it is lost or retired.

column4: browser to api, pending sign-in, memory
column5: A pending sign-in is consumed by its callback, or replaced by a newer sign-in from the same browser.
column6: A 30-minute bound, and a 1024-record cap that evicts the record closest to expiry, also end it.
column7: An abandoned sign-in produces no fact the api could observe. The bound frees the memory and is at least the realm's login and login-action page timeouts; it is a safety net, not a state transition.
column9: An abandoned sign-in emits a fact the api can observe.

column4: restore, HTTPS
column5: One custody check, gated by an authenticated session.
column6: Phase 1 of restore runs with no session.
column7: Before a restore there is no account, so there is nobody to authenticate. Phase 1's gate is C03's predicate, both clauses (no first-run claim and no pre-update user row); it is the only gate that exists at that point.
column9: A surface exists that can authenticate the operator before any account exists.

column4: device to mesh admission, HTTPS
column5: One mint function.
column6: Two profiles, one for a node and one for a user device.
column7: A node key is single-use, carries the node tag and is expired when the enrol step ends. A user key carries the user-device tag, refuses node tags, is capped and is shown once. The two differ in every field that decides authority.
column9: Node and user devices are admitted with the same tag set and the same lifecycle.

column4: control plane key material, local
column5: One key per trust root.
column6: The control plane holds five: the bus key, the controlplane CA, the store CA, the identity CA and the realm signing key. It holds six once radius.enable mints the network-access CA.
column7: They root different things and are presented to different verifiers. Merging any two would make one compromise reach what both root: the bus, every browser and node that trusts the controlplane CA, the secret store, whose listener trusts the store CA alone, and the identity service, whose listeners trust the identity CA alone. The store CA also issues the seal rotation's and the store provisioner's client leaves (C21, C22), and its api client leaf has CN rasputin-api, the subject the identity service admits as its administrator, so the identity CA cannot be the store CA.
column9: The bus, the controlplane HTTPS services, the secret store and the identity service are verified against one trust root.

column4: node to control plane, client auth, NATS
column5: A credential ends when a fact ends it, and revoke forces the disconnect.
column6: The minted connection credential also lapses after 24 hours.
column7: The lapse covers a missed forced disconnect. On reconnect the client re-presents its token and the registry is read again, so the bound is a safety net that re-checks a fact rather than a clock that decides one.
column9: Revoke confirms every session drop, so a missed disconnect becomes a detectable fact.

column4: agent to control plane, backup transfer, HTTPS
column5: The transfer grant is valid while the operation is open.
column6: The grant also carries a lifetime.
column7: The lifetime is derived from the operation's own work budget plus slack, and covers an operation that ends without closing its grant.
column9: An operation that ends always emits the fact that closes its grant.

column4: device to mesh admission, node profile
column5: The node key is expired explicitly when the enrol step ends, on success or failure.
column6: The key also carries a 10-minute expiry.
column7: It covers an api that stops mid-step, when nothing is left running to issue the explicit expiry.
column9: The enrol step's end is durable across an api restart.

column4: third-party verification of our leaves, TLS
column5: A credential is ended by a fact.
column6: Application and server leaves are bounded only by their expiry.
column7: Browsers and the tailnet client verify these leaves, and Rasputin publishes no revocation list, so expiry is the only bound those verifiers can apply. A copy taken off the node stays valid to them until then.
column9: Rasputin publishes a revocation list those verifiers consult.

column4: join token mint, out of band
column5: One mint path.
column6: The seed is minted two ways: offline for a matched set, or online through the add-node flow under a session.
column7: The offline path has to work with no control plane reachable at all. The online path has to bind a node id the operator chose in the interface.
column9: One path can mint a seed both offline and under a session.

column4: archive key wrap, local
column5: One custody key-derivation resolver.
column6: Two derivations: a memory-hard one for a human passphrase, a fast one for a generated recovery code.
column7: The cost parameter follows the secret's entropy. A full-entropy generated code gains nothing from a memory-hard derivation, and a human-chosen passphrase needs one.
column9: The recovery code and the passphrase carry the same entropy.

column4: mesh admin, local
column5: One admin channel.
column6: A container exec to the local socket is kept, used only to mint a short-lived REST key at each api start.
column7: The mesh server has no way to issue the first REST key over REST.
column9: The mesh server can issue an initial API key without local socket access.

column4: platform sidecar to host, unix socket
column5: A client is given a scoped credential for the service it talks to.
column6: The container socket is mounted into the collector sidecar.
column7: The collector's container discovery has no scoped equivalent in the daemon's API.
column9: The collector can discover containers with a scoped credential.

column4: custom compose to compute node, privilege check, Job
column5: A tile's compose reaches a compute node only at a privilege tier the catalog declares and the operator consents to.
column6: A custom compose runs unvalidated (ADR-0006 Decision 12).
column7: A custom compose is the owner's own configuration, which no catalog tier describes. Only apps.host holders, who are administrators, may submit one, or install or upgrade a host-trusting tile.
column9: A custom compose is privilege-checked.

column4: node configuration apply, local
column5: One apply sink and one key path.
column6: The OS and the firewall differ in both.
column7: The firewall's root filesystem is a read-only squashfs and its configuration sink is UCI and procd, not an env file and systemd. Neither difference is a choice.
column9: The firewall image carries a writable root filesystem and a systemd sink.

column4: OS bundle signature, artifact
column5: A detached CMS signature.
column6: The A/B update bundle carries its signature inside the bundle.
column7: The bundle format embeds the signature and the updater verifies it with its own keyring before we see the payload.
column9: The bundle format accepts a detached signature.

column4: CI signing, credential
column5: One signing credential.
column6: There are three: one for releases, one for the catalog, and the Super4C BMC firmware's RSA-3072 key.
column7: Separating them is what makes the purpose OIDs enforceable: a catalog leaf cannot sign a release and a release leaf cannot sign a catalog. The firmware key is separate because ESP32 over-the-air verification accepts only an RSA-3072 Secure Boot V2 signature checked by key digest, which the release leaf (ECDSA P-384 X.509 with purpose OIDs) cannot produce.
column9: One credential can carry both purposes without either being able to sign the other's artifacts. For the firmware key: an ESP32 over-the-air verifier that accepts the release leaf's scheme.

column4: release selection, HTTPS
column5: Every field of a release selection comes from the verified manifest.
column6: The channel comes from an unsigned flag.
column7: The prerelease flag is a property of the hosting platform's release object, not of the signed manifest. A signed channel value may only narrow it.
column9: The manifest carries a signed channel value.

column4: browser to api, session, cookie
column5: A pre-update session (rasputin-session, the sessions table, read by hash) resolves only to its moved account while that account holds a designation: administrator while its moved designation stands, otherwise no console role. It never writes the old tables, and is ended by sign-out, by a new console sign-in clearing its cookie, and by C15's deletion on disable, removal or demotion.
column6: A 7-day absolute lifetime also ends it.
column7: A lost or retired laptop produces no fact the api can observe, so no checkable fact is available to end that session. This is the one credential bound here with nothing behind it.
column9: A signed-in device emits a fact the api can observe when it is lost or retired.

column4: first-flash integrity, laptop
column5: One verifier implementation.
column6: The laptop side is a shell check rather than the Go verifier.
column7: No Rasputin binary exists on the laptop at first flash. The laptop has openssl and nothing else we ship.
column9: A signed verifier binary is distributed with the flasher.

column4: package feeds, HTTPS
column5: One publisher trust root.
column6: The firewall image keeps the upstream distribution's feed signing keys.
column7: Conditional, and only while the package manager is kept. Rasputin never installs a package at runtime; only an operator does.
column9: The firewall image ships without a package manager.

column4: clock, NTP
column5: Every input to a trust decision is authenticated.
column6: Time is taken from unauthenticated NTP.
column7: No authenticated time source is available to an appliance on an arbitrary LAN with no operator configuration. What is narrowed instead is how much depends on the clock.
column9: An authenticated time source is available with no operator configuration.

column4: seed, physical
column5: A credential is authorized by a checkable fact.
column6: The seed's authority is physical possession of the medium it arrives on.
column7: Nothing exists on a node before the seed that could authenticate it, so possession is the only fact available at that point.
column9: A node can authenticate a seed before it holds any credential.

column4: secrets at rest, filesystem
column5: One helper decides the mode of every file a process writes.
column6: The api and the agent each carry their own copy of that helper.
column7: The api's package is internal to a different Go module, so the agent binary cannot import it at all. The copy keeps the same semantics for every name both packages share and carries only what the agent uses.
column9: The helper lives in a module both binaries already import.

column4: release selection, HTTPS
column5: Every field of a release selection comes from a manifest this api verified against the trust root for the release purpose.
column6: A release below its component's version floor is resolved WITHOUT reading its signature, so its version, asset names and checksums are taken on HTTPS alone.
column7: Releases published before the release purpose OID existed are signed by a leaf that carries no extendedKeyUsage at all, which the verifier refuses by construction. Measured, not assumed: rasputin-os 2026.08.3 and earlier are signed by `Rasputin Release Leaf 001` (no EKU); 2026.08.4 onward by `Rasputin Bundle Signing leaf-003`, which carries the release OID. Requiring verification below the floor would leave a cluster still running one of those releases unable to resolve the flashable image for its OWN version, so it could not add a node at all -- turning a stale-version problem into an onboarding outage. The narrowest difference this forces is per component and per version: at or above the floor a signature is REQUIRED and a missing one is a hard failure, so the exception cannot be used to downgrade a signed release by deleting its .sig.
column9: No supported release predates its component's floor.

column4: trust bundle delivery to a node, NATS
column5: A node takes its trust bundle on trust.install, its own verb, and no other command carries it.
column6: mesh.enroll still carries the bundle to an agent that predates trust.install, and the mesh reconcile re-delivers it to those agents, and only those, by re-running mesh.enroll.
column7: An agent below the trust.install floor has no subscription for the verb, and mesh.enroll is the only path by which it installs trust before tailscale up dials Headscale. Without it such a node gets no trust at enroll and none after an identity restore.
column9: Every registered node reports an agent version at or above the trust.install floor.

column4: api to identity service, client auth, TLS
column5: The api presents its identity-CA client leaf, and the administrator client authenticates it by client-x509 on its exact subject (C27).
column6: identity.recover_admin, a system job, has Keycloak's bootstrap-admin service command make a temporary master-realm client, rasputin-recover-<job id>, authenticated by a client secret, and uses it to re-create rasputin-admin.
column7: The command is Keycloak's only way back in once rasputin-admin is gone or broken, and the client it makes takes a client secret and nothing else, so client-x509 cannot be set on it. The narrowest difference is per job: the secret is 32 random bytes made for that job, held in process memory and handed to the command only on the recovery launcher's standard input, into the command's own environment, never an argument or a file; the job deletes every temporary client before it reports restored, and fails if it cannot.
column9: Keycloak's bootstrap-admin service command can make a client authenticated by client-x509.

column4: human trust in the controlplane CA, out of band
column5: A trust anchor is verified against a surface the person already trusts.
column6: No device verifies the controlplane CA out of band; every device takes it on first use.
column7: Recorded decision. A fingerprint comparison surface was considered and not taken, because it adds a step to every device for a value the operator cannot check independently.
column9: The provisioning tool mints the controlplane CA for a matched set and the preseed carries a first-run claim code.

column4: origin enforcement, HTTPS (identity-service front channel)
column5: The api enforces one origin allowlist for the console, through cross-origin protection over the console's own origins (C02).
column6: The identity service's front channel is served at the two sign-in doors, each with its own controls instead: cross-origin protection with no bypass at the home door and one bypass, a SAML POST, at the app door; a per-door path allowlist; the door's own script policy per page class; no HSTS; and the cookie rules both ways.
column7: The doors serve another site's pages (sso-<cid>.local, signin.<cid>.internal), which the console's allowlist must never hold, and a SAML device posts its binding from its own site. The narrowest difference is per door and per path: only the app door's POST to protocol/saml bypasses cross-origin protection, and every other path the doors do not allowlist answers 404.
column9: The identity service's front channel is no longer served through the api.

column4: browser to identity service, guessing, HTTPS
column5: A state change follows a checkable fact, never a clock.
column6: A source address that keeps failing to sign in waits a rising 60 to 900 seconds at each door, counted from the drained failure events over a 12-hour window, beside Keycloak's per-account backstop of 100 failures over 12 hours with the quick check off. UNLOCK clears the person's attack-detection record and ends no source's wait; a source's wait ends on its own bound (C19, register label N9).
column7: Guessing produces no fact that says it has stopped, and a per-account lockout lets two requests a minute keep any account locked. The bounds are clock bounds Bryce ratified on 2026-11-02 (D22). The narrowest difference: only credential posts from the waiting source at the one door are refused, one at a time per source, and every other address, passkey sign-in and password reset is unaffected.
column9: The doors throttle guessing on a fact rather than a wait.

column4: browser to identity service, forgotten password, HTTPS
column5: A password is changed only by someone who signs in as the account: its password and, for a privileged account, its second step.
column6: A recovery code alone resets a household account's password at its door's own reset client, with no email; a privileged account also gives a passkey, security key or authenticator code. The reset mints no session and ends every identity and console session of the person.
column7: Rasputin sends no email (D11), so a person who forgot their password and holds no passkey has no other way back but an administrator. The narrowest difference: one code, used once, at the door's own reset client only, and a privileged account still needs a factor that is not on its code sheet.
column9: A reset path that needs no recovery-code sheet becomes available.

column4: browser to api, authenticate, HTTPS (the move's bridge)
column5: A pre-update passkey, checked against rasputin.db with user verification required, yields a single-use grant bound to its moved account and the browser's host-only cookie. The grant authorizes only that account's first password and email (accounts.set_first_password) and opens no session. The password is typed on the console origin once.
column6: A 15-minute bound and a 1024-record cap also end a grant.
column7: Keycloak cannot resolve the 16-byte handles; D11 rules out email.
column9: Every moved account holds a password and no slot can boot a pre-identity api.

column4: node to control plane, client auth
column5: One credential authenticates the node to the control plane.
column6: NATS authenticates with the join token; HTTPS authenticates with a separately registered key.
column7: Recorded decisions: mutual TLS was put out of scope on the bus, and a persisted signing key for node identity was superseded. The HTTPS side must not carry the long-lived join token as a bearer.
column9: The bus requires TLS on every cluster, which holds from the release that deleted the plaintext ladder (geekdojo/geekdojo-brain#517): the callout can now accept the registered key, and NATS keep the token only for first registration.

column4: node process to mesh, server trust, HTTPS
column5: A process is given its trust root through its own configuration.
column6: The tailnet client is given the node trust bundle through an environment variable.
column7: That variable is the only hook the client's runtime offers for a per-process trust root; it exposes no configuration option for one.
column9: The tailnet client exposes a configuration option for its trust root.

column4: browser to api, authenticate, HTTPS
column5: The console session from a sign-in through the home door (C70).
column6: A one-time repair code, made by root on the control plane with rasputin-api repair-code, opens one repair-only session that may read the sign-in service's state and restart it (identity.restart), reset one administrator's or designated account's sign-in once (accounts.repair_reset, C1), and, only while the identity service holds no accounts and rasputin.db holds pre-update accounts and a move record, run the move again (identity.move, C9); every other route answers 403.
column7: D12: credentials live only in the identity service, so when it is down, or every administrator has lost every way in while it works, no sign-in can authenticate anyone. Only the code's SHA-256 is kept, in memory, and never in a URL; one code and one session at a time; five wrong codes refuse a source; refused at both sign-in doors; one reset per session, confirmed by name; the move's re-run confirmed by its count and decided by the kind table on C9's state; recorded under the actor break-glass with a critical alert, and the reset with its own.
column9: The identity service can authenticate someone while its process or its database is down.

column4: origin enforcement, HTTPS (break-glass)
column5: One normalized origin allowlist, the console's own (C02, C71).
column6: A repair code is redeemed, and its session used, at https://<cid>.local or at https://<the control plane's primary LAN address>, by a check of its own; the session is bound to the origin it was opened at, and an Origin header must equal the request's own. The console's allowlist never gains the address.
column7: When the console's name does not resolve on the device (no mDNS on that device or that LAN), the address is the only way to reach the control plane, and the last resort must not depend on name resolution (SO §8.4).
column9: Every device on the LAN reaches the console by its name whenever it reaches the control plane at all.
